list.name: Dia-thìr
list.note: For nine centuries one hand has held both the vein and the realm, and Lagh an Loscaidh Bhig has not changed. At the close of the age the crown is empty and Comhairle a' Chùraim sits in its place. Ruled by Comhairle a' Chùraim (high custodian Tormod mac Ailein, first named in AE 2). Told of in: The crown and the custody joined (LE 859); The custody's seal on the king's letters (LE 865); The Council of Custodians grants leave (AE 2).

1.note: A strait harbour of Dia-thìr. Its people keep the rite of Òrd na Cloiche. The small walled harbour on the south-west coast beside Inis thais kept a harbour shrine that the priests of Òrd an t-Seabhaig and an Fhianna both came to claim in LE 427, their feast mornings falling on the same day. The king's reeve, Murchadh mac Ailpein, halved the shrine's hours between them, as the sacred woods of an older age had once been divided, and nailed the division on a strip of hide to the shrine door. The division held, and neither order was pleased with it. Known for the shrine with two orders' hours. Told of in: Òrd an t-Seabhaig and an Fhianna claim the same feast day at Caol leathan (LE 427); Hawk and wolf at Caol leathan (LE 429); Murchadh mac Ailpein divides the shrine's days (LE 429).

3.note: A farm town of Dia-thìr. The south-eastern town's dyers made a fast blue from a marsh plant and a mordant of their own, and in LE 1,064 the dyer Oighrig nic Ailein, after ten years changing one thing at a time, found the mixing that held the blue through washing after washing; cloth of it was worn at Taigh na Fèithe's midwinter gathering within the year and became the feast-day dress of the custodian houses. The last dyer who knew the mordant quarrelled with both her apprentices and died without teaching either, and the blue that followed, though it kept the old name, was the common blue of the rest of the island; the old weavers held the two lengths side by side and mourned the difference aloud for the rest of their lives. Known for the Baile ghorm blue, and its losing. Told of in: The blue dyers of Baile ghorm (LE 1,064); Oighrig nic Ailein fixes Baile ghorm's blue (LE 1,064); The Baile ghorm blue fades (LE 1,139).

17.note: A town of Dia-thìr: the grain fleet of the cold way (laid up LE 1,634) and a house of disputation. Its people keep the rite of Scoiltean nan Draoidhean. The river town of the north built barges in the second century of the count to carry grain down the Abhainn ghorm and west along the cold way of the north coast, and a boy of the town watching the first one loaded asked his father why it should not simply cross open water by the shorter way, and got a look and no answer. Pupils of Dùn thais founded a house of disputation here in LE 769, the question of the vein argued in the north for the first time. The great gale of LE 1,229 drove the sea up the river higher than anyone living had seen and heaped the strand with broken plank. As the roads improved the coasting trade went by cart, and in LE 1,634 the last barge that had worked the cold way was hauled above the tide-line and chocked level, kept rather than broken up, though few of the town's fathers could say any longer what the cold way had been the way from. Known for the grain barges of the cold way, and the last one kept on the strand. Told of in: Inis mhòr's grain fleet (LE 154); The druid school at Inis mhòr (LE 769); The great gale at Inis mhòr (LE 1,229); Inis mhòr's grain fleet laid up (LE 1,634); A boy of Inis mhòr asks why the barges keep the coast (LE 130).

19.note: A town of Dia-thìr. Seat of the crown and of Comhairle a' Chùraim; the tally-houses, the firlot, Clàr nan Rìghrean; the lesser town beside Cathair mhòr. Its people keep the rite of Òrd Mhacha. The kings and queens of the age kept their hall on An Cnoc Ruadh above the Abhainn dhomhain, and every crowning of the age was made there. Beathag nic Dhòmhnaill heard the three crews in An Talla Dearg in the first year, gave her word that the crown would send no one and keep no one back, and wore undyed wool for her sister from the thirteenth year of the count until she died in the fifty-fifth. The houses first chose a king here when Ìomhar's line failed, in a cold yard where seven neck-rings caught the sun and nobody spoke for a morning. Sìleas set the standard firlot here and widened the bridge for two carts abreast; Catrìona Bhuadhach laid her stone road south from it to Inis thais. The crown was joined to the mastery of Taigh na Fèithe in Dòmhnall Ruadh's reign, and from then An Talla Dearg's letters carried the custody's seal. The capital grew slowly and Cathair mhòr passed it in the tenth century of the count; in the age's last years the hall held perhaps five hundred souls. After Queen Gormshuil went up to the winter burning in LE 1,795 and nothing more is told, Na Seachd Taighean sat at her board with her chair left empty, and named themselves Comhairle a' Chùraim there in LE 1,812. Known for An Talla Dearg, the queen's empty chair, and the board of Na Seachd Taighean. Told of in: Queen Sìleas's measures (LE 261); Tally-houses in the royal granaries (LE 284); Cathair mhòr the largest town (LE 969); The Council of Custodians grants leave (AE 2); The tidings at Cathair dhearg (LE 1); The Cuan shean crew heard in An Talla Dearg (LE 1); The Ros bheag crew heard in An Talla Dearg (LE 1); The Ceann mhòr crew heard in An Talla Dearg (LE 1); Murchadh's leaf of the three tellings (LE 1); How many days' water (LE 1).

20.note: A town of Dia-thìr: the first house of Òrd an t-Seabhaig and Leabhar an t-Seabhaig; An Seabhag Acrach kept its house here after the schism. Its people keep the rite of Òrd an t-Seabhaig. The walled town above Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag kept the dawn-hawk rite of An Aois Naomh, and in the third century of the count the priestess Gormshuil nic Artair taught there that the hawk of the rite was Mòd himself, and that the vein under Muileann dhearg was a hawk of his kind, to be fed the measured handful and never glutted past it. Her father Artair kept the mews before her; she first called the hawk down alone at three-and-thirty. Her watchers raised Taigh an t-Seabhaig below the mews block in LE 232, and after her death Ùisdean mac Pàdraig wrote her sayings as Leabhar an t-Seabhaig. By royal grant in LE 471 Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag passed to the priests of Macha alone. At the council of Òrd an t-Seabhaig here in LE 889 a young priest asked whether Mòd would rather starve a grown flock than see his handful grown to meet it, and those who held he would not were named An Seabhag Biadhte and asked to keep their teaching elsewhere. In the eleventh century the priest Tòmas mac Aonghais cleared the moss from Carragh Cnoc bheag above the town with wooden scrapers and found letters no table of the schools could read. Known for the house of Òrd an t-Seabhaig and Leabhar an t-Seabhaig. Told of in: Gormshuil of the Hawk (LE 229); The sayings of Gormshuil written (LE 251); The schism of the Hawk (LE 889); A hawk overfed will not come to the glove (LE 215); Gormshuil calls Mòd down alone for the first time (LE 218); Death of Artair, hawk-keeper of Cnoc bheag (LE 220); Gormshuil first names the vein An Seabhag Acrach (LE 221); Hawk-keepers of the north coast come to hear her (LE 225); Bàgh an t-Seabhaig elder questions Gormshuil's own hunger (LE 225).

23.note: A city of Dia-thìr: the largest town on the island since LE 969: the market of all the south, Macha's great house with its floor of black and white, the copper-workers. Its people keep the rite of Òrd Mhacha. The walled market city of the south took in forty-one burnt-out households of Doire mhin in LE 555 at the temple of Macha and fed them through the winter on the temple's grain without asking whose claim they had favoured. In the winter of the refusal its temple fire went out in Dubhlas, on a morning so still the smoke of the last coals stood upright, and when a carrier's basket brought coal again it was the first of the cold shires' hearths to burn. Its market drew the trade of all the south, and a carter asked why he sold his barley here and not at the capital said a man carries his load to whichever gate opens first and pays best; by LE 969 it was greater than the capital. Its copper-workers stamped every cooking pot with a maker's mark and sent them out on every road. It fed Ceann mhin after the burning of Cogadh nam Bràithrean, and in the fifteenth century the priests of Macha finished their great house here, its floor of black and white eleven years in the laying, the largest roofed building on Dia-thìr. Known for Macha's great house, and the copper pots of every hearth. Told of in: Cathair mhòr the largest town (LE 969); The copper-workers of Cathair mhòr (LE 994); Macha's great house at Cathair mhòr (LE 1,459); The Doire mhin folk at Cathair mhòr (LE 555); The temple fires of the cold shires go out (LE 558); The verse of the cold shires (LE 559); The first hearth relit (LE 560); The witness of Doire mhin heard in full (LE 618).

24.note: A headland harbour of Dia-thìr. Its people keep the rite of Òrd an t-Seabhaig. The harbour town on the north coast took the dawn rite of Òrd an t-Seabhaig in LE 239, when two of Gormshuil nic Artair's pupils, a brother and sister of a coastal household, carried it down from Cnoc bheag so that the fishing families need not walk two days inland for it; Gormshuil came down herself to judge whether the teaching had travelled whole. Its hawk-house took charge of the measured burning for the country between the coast and the hills, and was eight years old when Gormshuil died. Ùisdean mac Pàdraig came here to gather what her pupils remembered for Leabhar an t-Seabhaig, and marked every saying he had not heard from her own mouth. Known for the second house of Òrd an t-Seabhaig. Told of in: The hawk-house at Ros gheal (LE 239); A second house raised at Ros gheal (LE 239).

26.note: A town with a landing of Dia-thìr. Its people keep the rite of Òrd Mhacha. Catrìona nic Aonghais came against it in the autumn of LE 556; borrowed fishing coasters shut its water gate by night while her lines held the land gate. With no ground beyond the walls for burying, the dead were laid near the well-heads, and a sickness of the gut went through the streets and the garrison. On the fortieth day Niall Mòr mac Leòid surrendered, and Catrìona let his garrison march out between her silent lines on his sworn word, carrying its dead and wounded by name. It was in her camp before this city that Dùghall Garbh came with six men and no herald to offer her his host against Raghnall Ruadh. Known for the siege of forty days and the garrison freed on oath. Told of in: Catrìona's answer to the ford (LE 554); The water gate of Cathair dhomhain is closed (LE 556); The wells of Cathair dhomhain foul (LE 557); The garrison of Cathair dhomhain freed on oath (LE 557); The siege of Cathair dhomhain (LE 557); The pact of Catrìona and Dùghall (LE 559).

30.note: A town of Dia-thìr. Burned twice: by Alasdair Bàn's ships in Cogadh nam Bràithrean and by the great fire of LE 1,549; rebuilt with gable walls of stone. Its people keep the rite of Òrd Mhacha. The walled harbour city declared for Iain Ciar in Cogadh nam Bràithrean, and in LE 1,272 Alasdair Bàn's ships came down the coast and burned its waterfront before the town's own bell had finished ringing the alarm. The fire took the tarred rope stores and then the granary; by the second morning the town had lost both what it needed to put to sea and what it needed to eat until harvest. Cathair mhòr, which had taken no side, sent grain enough that no household went hungry that winter. In LE 1,549 a second great fire burned it with no war to blame, and before the ash had cooled its reeve ordered it rebuilt with gable walls of stone between each house and the next, so that a fire must cross stone to spread. Known for its two fires, and the gable walls. Told of in: The fire at Ceann mhin (LE 1,272); The fire of Ceann mhin (LE 1,549); Ceann mhin's reeve orders the gable walls (LE 1,549).

32.note: A ford village of Dia-thìr. Its people keep the rite of Òrd Mhacha. The walled ford town on the river above the granaries keeps the old crossing of the eastern road. In LE 554 Dùghall Garbh, guided by drovers who had used a hidden ford above the town for forty years to move cattle untolled, crossed his host in the dark and broke Raghnall Ruadh's camp at the ford; Leabhar a' Chùraim counts some three hundred dead, most of them drowned, and one old soldier swore to Seònaid nic Coinnich that the fighting took two days, not one. In the seventeenth century the growers on the slopes above the ford began to press blaeberry and bramble into a dark wine that kept a year in the cask, and the road-houses of the eastern stretch took to serving it as black wine. Known for the ford of Cogadh nan Trì Tagraichean, and the black wine. Told of in: The ford at Àth shean (LE 554); Dùghall crosses the shallows by night (LE 554); The dark wine of Àth shean (LE 1,626); The road-houses take up the black wine (LE 1,626).

34.note: A large village of Dia-thìr: the ancestor shrine and its feast-market of honey and wax lights. Its people keep the rite of Scoiltean nan Draoidhean. The small citadel harbour of the east kept an ancestor shrine of Na Seann Spioradan, and from LE 644 the crowds that came to it for the great feasts held a market on the three feast days, chiefly of honey, beeswax for the shrine's lights and the wool of the hill farms. The market outgrew the feasts in time and was held whether the shrine had a feast or not. Known for the feast-market at the shrine. Told of in: The feast-market at Seann Tarr (LE 644).

35.note: A hamlet of Dia-thìr. Grove village with a landing. Its people keep the rite of Òrd Mhacha. A wood of wild oak, crooked and never anyone's grove, stood on the shore of Loch chrom below the capital, and in the fifth year woodcutters of the roll built huts at its edge to fell crooked oak for the fleet's frames and knees. The huts did not outlast the felling. The wood kept its name, and the tellers of that shore say that timber for the fleet was felled there. Fifteen centuries on, other woodcutters came to what was left of the wood and stayed, and their huts became the village of Doire fhiadhaich, a fishing and cutting place on the capital shore that remembered the fleet chiefly as a reason for its name. Known for its oaks, said to have built a' Scaradh fleet. Told of in: Woodcutters' huts at Doire fhiadhaich (LE 5).

36.note: A large village of Dia-thìr. Harbour on an Old Ones' site. Its people keep the rite of Òrd Mhacha. The harbour town on the south coast below the mountain finished its stone mole in LE 899, and the coal-barges of the mountain roads tied up there where before they had beached on shingle at low water; it became the port of the coal-carts coming down to the coast towns of the south. After Cogadh nam Bràithrean Alasdair Bàn held its lordship for life under the peace, kept the peace he had made to the end of his days, and died here in LE 1,291. The lordship returned to the crown, and Iain Ciar left it vacant for the rest of his reign. Known for the coal mole, and the lordship left vacant. Told of in: The harbour of Seann Chwen (LE 899); The first barges tie up at Seann Chwen's new mole (LE 900); Death of Alasdair Bàn (LE 1,291); Iain Ciar keeps his brother's lordship vacant (LE 1,291).

37.note: A village of Dia-thìr. Harbour on an Old Ones' site. The harbour town of the north coast lost its old harbour wall in one night in LE 259, in the storm its fishers call Am Fuath Mòr, and with it forty boats at their moorings and eighteen men and women who had gone down in the dark to save them. Its young reeve, Raghnall mac Nèill, thirty-four and four years in office, stood knee-deep hauling on a rope to bring in a boat with two children lashed inside, and afterward lost his count twice burying the dead in a single row on the headland. Known for the hooked harbour wall. Told of in: The storm that took Seann Toll's boats (LE 259); Raghnall mac Nèill in the water at Seann Toll (LE 259); The dead of Am Fuath Mòr buried on the headland (LE 259); Seann Toll walls its harbour again (LE 261).

49.note: A strait harbour of Dia-thìr. Its people keep the rite of Òrd Mhanannain. The fishing town on the wild strait near Inis thais was founded in LE 739. Its fishers had always kept their boats inside the strait that gave the town its name, never past their own headlands, until in LE 1,389 some of them went out and found a safe lane south to the landing at Cidhe Beag. Slighe-mhara Caol fhiadhaich was not believed at first; within a season or two of its being believed, the older harbours of the south coast followed it one after another. Known for Slighe-mhara Caol fhiadhaich. Told of in: The southern lane (LE 1,389).

55.note: A river-island village of Dia-thìr. Its people keep the rite of Òrd Mhanannain. The fishing village a little below Seann Skell gave more households to Rolla nan Deònach than any other place on the island. Two of its households said in the drying-shed, in the first year, that they would go if a boat were ever built that could make the crossing, and the village laughed and then stopped laughing. Mòrag nic Dhòmhnaill and her husband Aonghas mac Fhionnlaigh farmed the land above it, and it was at their board that Alasdair Saor was sent north to the oaks of Doire fhionn. When An Fhaoileag An Fhaoileag lay down off Ros àrsaidh in the sixth year, its boats brought back three living and eight dead. When the broken tidings of two landfalls came, the village kept both halves of the tale at once. Ruairidh mac Artair had a deep hull built here in the fourth century of the count; it listed at launch and was broken up within a fortnight, for no wright still living held the old scarfing of the keel. Told of in: Two households of Inis àrsaidh (LE 1); Aonghas mac Fhionnlaigh says yes (LE 2); Mòrag undertakes to pay for the oaks (LE 4); The trial hull lost off Ros àrsaidh (LE 6); The nine named at Inis àrsaidh (LE 6); The keening at Inis àrsaidh (LE 6).

63.note: A headland harbour of Dia-thìr. Its people keep the rite of Òrd Mhanannain. The walled harbour town of the Ros bheag cape sent its skipper Oighrig nic Raghnaill to An Talla Dearg in the first year with a telling of a high forested coast past the north cape, and two of the six pilots who walked east to learn the stars at Cuan ruadh were its own, Catrìona nic Iain among them. After the sailing it was a fishing and coasting town like its neighbours. Manannan's teaching came to it down the coast with the fishing families, and in LE 694 the priests of the order at Ros bheag laid down that no boat of the faithful might go out of sight of the headlands; within the year two of the order's boats turned back its own skipper Coinneach mac Sheumais when he chased a run of fish too far. Four years later a priest there asked a pilot's grandson, Griogair, which star his grandfather had steered by, and the boy could not say. The rule of the headlands was kept on the west coast for the rest of the age. Known for the rule of sight-of-land, and the pilot who forgot his star. Told of in: The pilot of Ros bheag (LE 1); Six pilots sent east to Cuan ruadh (LE 11); Manannan's order at Ros bheag and Cuan shean (LE 674); Within sight of land (LE 694); The rule of the headlands laid down (LE 694); Coinneach mac Sheumais turned back within the year (LE 694).

64.note: A town of Dia-thìr. Kept its gates shut to all three claimants and holds its own gates and tolls by grant. Its people keep the rite of Òrd Mhanannain. The walled port nearest the capital on the west keeps salt-pans and brine springs behind its walls, and they fed it through Cogadh nan Trì Tagraichean. Its reeve Mairead nic Ruairidh gave the heralds of all three claimants the same answer at the western gate: the town would open to trade and shut to hosts until the houses agreed which claim to answer. Dùghall Garbh sat before it a fortnight in LE 553, and Mairead sold his host bread at the market rate until his carters cost him more than the town was worth; he came back better provisioned three years later and sat a month, and marched away when Catrìona closed the gates of Cathair dhomhain. In LE 594 Catrìona Bhuadhach granted Seann Warr the right to keep its own gates and take its own tolls, and the grant was cut in stone letters over the landward gate. Known for the gate shut against all three claimants, and the grant cut over it. Told of in: Seann Warr shuts its gates (LE 553); Seann Warr's gates honoured (LE 594); Mairead nic Ruairidh bars the gate to all three (LE 552); Seann Warr's first siege (LE 553); Seann Warr's second siege (LE 556); Seann Warr's grant cut over the gate (LE 594).

67.note: A ford village of Dia-thìr. Its people keep the rite of Òrd Mhacha. The granary town south of the mountain kept the crown's stores. In the grain strife of LE 37 its reeve, Tormod mac Coinnich, who remembered a store-house swept empty behind a smiling reeve when he was seven, barred the granary doors and set a watch of four on them through Samhnas, Dubhlas and the black months, turning away every petitioner until a single rider came in Sìolach with a word that the grain might move; how the strife was settled he was never told. The middle pier of its bridge was rebuilt in stone in LE 46. Sìleas's firlot settled its first quarrel here, a carter and a miller measured true before the crowd their shouting drew. In LE 699 the granaries, standing since before a' Scaradh, were pulled down and built again in dressed stone on raised floors against the rats, under the reeve Fearchar mac Phàdraig. Eight centuries after that a young clerk found the town's firlot worn smaller than the capital's standard, and had been for generations. Known for the barred granary, and the worn firlot. Told of in: Tormod mac Coinnich remembers the dearth of his boyhood (LE 37); A lean harvest in the south shires (LE 37); Petitioners come to the barred granary (LE 37); The watch stands through the winter (LE 37); Àth shean shuts its granaries (LE 38); The granary doors reopened (LE 38).

76.note: A large village of Dia-thìr. Once the richest place in the north-east on its salt (the fair of LE 959); its river silted, it keeps the market-court on the headland. Its people keep the rite of Scoiltean nan Draoidhean. The small walled river town of the north-east found its fortune in LE 350, when a farmer digging a ditch above it struck warm water that tasted of salt. Pans were laid out on the flats within the season, and the salt went inland over Drochaid Ros fhionn, whose keeper Iain mac Ùisdein took a handful from every load for his toll and filled an iron-bound salt-box faster than any box on that road. Ros fhionn salted the fish of the mining shires, and at the height of its fair in LE 959 the reeve lost his count past four thousand people on the flats. The salt-masters rebuilt the bridge's arches at their own cost in the twelfth century after a carter's mule went into the river through the road bed. Then a shifting bar silted the Abhainn bheag, the barges could no longer reach the quays, and the salt went by sea through Caol gharbh; the market-court stayed on its headland with its bench of old oak, the bridge's last keeper died with no one to take the toll, and the channel was withied from the bar to open water. Known for its salt, its bridge and its market-court. The walled temple city in the north-east is the seat of Taigh na Deasbaid. Coinneach mac Mhàrtainn, a druid of the schools of Flidais who had walked the carters' roads for forty years, raised Taigh na Deasbaid here in LE 314 and had the schools' old question, Carson an làmh seo?, cut into its lintel before the roof was on. Pupils walked three days from Caol bheag to sit its benches. In LE 324 Coinneach asked there whether the hands that went with the fleet were those the vein answered best, and each of Na Seachd Taighean forbade the question at its own table. Ailean mac Dhùghaill's tables of the three old ruins were judged here, and in the thirteenth century Raghnall mac Chaluim set out here Clàr nam Bliadhnachan that showed the heads of the houses living longer than their tenants; the table was forbidden and the house shut. It was opened and shut more than once, and last reopened in LE 1,759 on condition that the question of longer lives never be raised; its schools turned instead to whether Leabhar a' Chùraim's handful answered to what the coal gave out. Known for Taigh na Deasbaid, and the questions it was forbidden. 119.note: A large village of Dia-thìr: a second harbour arm for the boats of Seann Tarr; the star-lore of its old steersmen, now lost. The eastern harbour, a hundred miles from the west coast over the mountain country, kept the only sailors of the island who had ever held a course by night. Six pilots of the west walked to it in LE 11 and were sent to the old steersman Seumas Reultach, who taught them on the headland above the town the wheel of the sky and Reul na Stiùire, and had his granddaughter cut part of it on a hide; he died on the cliff path in LE 14 and is buried among his own people. After the pilots went west nobody at Cuan ruadh sailed by night any longer. In the fifteenth century it built a second harbour arm to take the boats of Seann Tarr when that harbour broke, and throve on the fishing of both towns' waters for the rest of the age. Known for the star-steersmen, and its second harbour arm. 122.note: A headland harbour of Dia-thìr. Its people keep the rite of Òrd Mhanannain. The small walled harbour on the point below Ros bheag is where the ships of Inis àrsaidh put out to sea. The first finished hull, An Fhaoileag, was taken past it for her trial in the sixth year and lay down in a following sea off its headland with fourteen aboard. Eight years later its strand was the ground of the first night-steering trial, when Catrìona nic Iain, home from the steersmen of Cuan ruadh, took one boat out past the headland with every lantern doused and brought her in by Reul na Stiùire before the lantern-boat that hugged the shore. Half the town came down to see it fail. After the fleet sailed the point went back to the coasting trade and the fishing, and nobody out of it is recorded to have sailed by night again. Known for the loss of An Fhaoileag, and the first night steered by a star. Told of in: The first night-steering trial off Ros àrsaidh (LE 14).

A second tremor in LE 929 brought down a gallery on fourteen of the custodians' own labourers in the small hours of the morning shift. households of the mountain leave small stones at its foot on the day of the fall. In LE 361 the district took it as its cloth of mourning, worn plain through a household's season of loss as the whole island had once worn an Tùrsa Geal, and an Tùrsa Geal was kept in it in that country from then on. 132.note: A town of Dia-thìr. Walled, with a market inside the landward gate; amber of Bàgh an t-Seabhaig; An Seabhag Biadhte's refuge. Its people keep the rite of Òrd an t-Seabhaig. The northern Seann Skell, on the bay the hawk-keepers call their own, is not the river port of the west. In the fifth century of the count it put up a wall around its streets for the first time, and the crown granted a market inside the new landward gate where the amber of that coast was sold beside whale-oil, honey and the wool of the northern moors; the amber-workers swore to sell no rough stone outside the walls, and one of them, Ailig an Òir, forfeited a season's gathering to his own guild for breaking the oath within the year. After the schism of Òrd an t-Seabhaig the priests of An Seabhag Biadhte settled here, and under Beathag nic Sheumais built a following of four families into a school. From here in LE 919 she rode to Cathair dhearg to ask that the measured handful be raised by a quarter for the hearths of the north coast, and carried the refusal home in her own satchel; the house stood after exactly as it had before. Known for the amber market inside the gate, and the house of An Seabhag Biadhte. 143.note: A village of Dia-thìr: the watch from the headland (lapsed); the timber from beyond the mist came ashore here. Its people keep the rite of Òrd Mhanannain. The fishing town twenty miles up the coast from Seann Skell sent Tòmas mac Uilleim to An Talla Dearg in the first year with the telling that the far land lay behind the mist and could be smelt on some mornings. After the sailing Seonag nic Dhùghaill climbed its headland at first light in LE 66 and kept it through the day, and household after household took a turn after her; the custom was called Faire a' Chinn, and Seonag kept her own turns for forty years. The watch lapsed long before the age was out, and the fishing thinned with the rest of the north-west, until perhaps a dozen boats still put out from its shore. In LE 1,794 its fishers found a worked timber cast up, longer than any tree of the island and fastened with nails no smith of Dia-thìr had forged. In the last years of the age a fisher of the town, Oighrig nic Eachainn, rested on her oars past where the rule of sight-of-land allowed, saw a hard dark line beyond the grey for a few breaths, and turned for home and told only her mother. Known for Faire a' Chinn, and the timber out of the mist. 166.note: A town of Dia-thìr: the first temple to Lia Fàil by name, roofed with northern slate; Queen Catrìona's own town. Its people keep the rite of Òrd Mhanannain. The walled harbour city of the south-west coast kept an old wolf-stone called Clach, watched for generations by families who had forgotten why. In LE 405 a net-maker of the strand, Dòmhnall mac Ailein, thirty-five years old, began telling the men who mended nets beside him that the stone was Lia Fàil and its watchers an Fhianna, sworn to keep the island as a wolf keeps its range, and his hearers became Òrd na Cloiche. They raised the first temple on the island to Lia Fàil by name, roofed with northern slate the shipmaster Beathag nic Raoghnaill fetched by sea, and blew a horn at every turn of the tide. Dòmhnall taught on the strand five-and-thirty years and never took an office. Catrìona nic Aonghais was born here in LE 526 to the king's brother, and her mother kept her here rather than raise her at An Talla Dearg; as queen she laid Rathad na Banrighinn in stone from the capital to her own gate. In LE 1,389 Òrd na Cloiche's congregation divided over whether the dead might be prayed for at Clach; those who said no kept the temple. Known for the wolf-stone Clach and Òrd na Cloiche. 190.note: A harbour of Dia-thìr. Its people keep the rite of Òrd Mhanannain. King Tormod Bàn sent grain south before any asking came, and the town rebuilt a full street back from the old shore, on ground no telling said the sea had reached; the king rode down to see it, the one journey of his reign made for a storm's sake. In LE 1,754 the sea came over the waterfront a second time and flooded the moved street to its thresholds, and the town built a sea-wall. The town buried the boundary stones of the first street rather than break them up. Known for the street moved back from the sea, and the sea-wall. 246.note: A large village of Dia-thìr: the first paper mill; Beathag nic Thòmais's loft of old copies, left to the town on condition nothing in it be burned. Its people keep the rite of Scoiltean nan Draoidhean. The mill town on the hill road of the east had a widow's loft by the seventeenth century of the count. Beathag nic Thòmais, whose husband had owned its mill, began in LE 1,659 to buy old copies of Leabhar a' Chùraim and Rolla a' Chalaidh from houses that no longer read them, and in her loft a crown clerk found the only surviving copy of a custodians' ruling Taigh na Fèithe had lost to fire. In LE 1,674 Anna nic Coinnich began to make paper from rags at the town's ford, the first on Dia-thìr; Beathag carried it sixty miles to Taigh na Fèithe herself, and Leabhar a' Chùraim was copied onto it for the first time. Among her papers she found three copies of the tidings of the two landfalls that did not agree, copied all three fair, and chose none. She left the loft to the town when she died in LE 1,699, on condition that nothing in it be burned, and the town kept the condition; its unpaid keeper told a crown reeve that fifty years of neither office asking for the papers back was itself an answer. Known for the paper mill and the loft of Beathag nic Thòmais. Both shire seats carried home the boundary stones they had brought to argue their claims and set them unused into their own walls, where they stood for the rest of the age pointing at a line the water had already drawn. 261.note: A grove village of Dia-thìr. The village in the north took its name from the oak grove on the hill above it, and in the fifth year Alasdair Saor came up the north road to fell it for the keels of the fleet. Its keeper, Eilidh nic Ruairidh, made him choose each tree he would take and hear its name; he chose fifty-four and left one young oak, the Child. Eighty men of the roll felled the grove through the summer, the greatest tree, the Queen, taking two days to bring down, and the keel-timbers went forty-two miles south to the sea on sleds of oak shod with ash, six yoke to a sled, over a causeway built across the stream below the village. The grove never grew again. The village built a low wall of stones round the Child, and its old keeper sat beside it every evening until dark. In LE 109 Taigh na Fèithe set down the coppice law of Doire fhionn, and the village lived thereafter by cutting coppice rather than oak, some of the fellowship's released journeymen among its cutters. Known for the oaks felled for the fleet, and the Child walled on the hill. 273.note: A town of Dia-thìr. Clann Fhearchair's town and the king's second court near the mountain; the white stone of its hills. Its people keep the rite of Scoiltean nan Draoidhean. The walled town near Taigh na Fèithe is the hall of Clann Fhearchair. Fearchar mac Lachlainn was born here, the elder son, and bound as a boy to a custodian's household for seven years while his younger brother Iain was kept at home to learn the hall; when the houses chose Fearchar king in LE 182, he kept his court part of each year here that he might take counsel of Taigh na Fèithe without a journey, and Iain kept Clann Fhearchair's hall when the court was at the capital. The brothers' letters across every season of the double court were gathered here into one leaf-book, boundary disputes beside a long complaint about the capital's cooking. Dùghall Garbh held his following here in the years before Cogadh nan Trì Tagraichean, and died here of the wound he took at Muileann chrom, his last words asking whether Taigh na Fèithe gates stood open. In the thirteenth century masons of Ceann leathan began to buy the veined white stone of the hills above the town, and its quarries were worked from then on. Known for the double court, and the hall of Clann Fhearchair. 282.note: A harbour of Dia-thìr. Its people keep the rite of Òrd Mhanannain. The harbour a dozen miles down the coast from Seann Skell heard the first tale of a far shore on its quays in the moon of Faolach of the first year, and its skipper Eachann mac Lachlainn told the queen of a low dark coast west and north of west. The walks turned off hands when the harbour trade halved after the sailing, and were shortened in the eighth century of the count, half the ground sown with barley. The rope-walker Tormod Ciar swore Cupa na Fìrinne on the walk itself, cupping rainwater in his hands. In the fourteenth century Tormod Ròpaire's crew still walked their strands to a work-song whose strange words named the parts of a deep keel, and Iseabail nic Lachlainn took it down there; the crew kept singing it exactly as he gave it, no better understood. Known for its rope-walks, and Òran na Druime. 288.note: A village of Dia-thìr: the potters of the grey-green glaze, lost with the last of Clann Mhic Phàil. White-stone millers raised the mill town in the south-east in LE 1,082 to grind for the city of Dùn dhearg. Its potters of Clann Mhic Phàil made a grey-green glaze that no other kiln could match, and the custodian houses bought their table-ware from that one family; the secret went mother to daughter unwritten. The last of the family, Iain Mac Phàil, took two apprentices in his last years, and neither learned to judge the moment the kiln's heat must be let fall. He died without passing it on in LE 1,509, and for a generation the town's potters tried to match it and failed. Known for the grey-green glaze, and its losing. At its first full-moon market traders came from three days' walk in every direction and carried honey, hemp, wax and pottery north as one company, and a trader of the long city asked the capital's clerk what stopped a false notch being cut after a bargain, and was shown how the grain of a split stick runs true only when its two halves are laid together. 305.note: A village of Dia-thìr. Half its houses empty since the sea-thieves and the poor harvests; its grain dues remitted. Its people keep the rite of Òrd Mhanannain. The north-west coast town was a quiet reeve's post until the sea-thieves of the small islands began boarding the coasters off its shore in the eighth century of the count. Its reeve Coinneach mac Nèill counted the going as carefully as he had counted grain, and in LE 789 reported half the houses empty, their thatch going to moss; the crown reckoned his town's dues by the households that stood. When the thieves put in twice in a moon within sight of his harbour he asked the crown for a force, and Eilidh Bhàn sent Iain mac Thormoid by sea; the town's own fishermen led the boats through the channel to Eilean dhubh, where the thieves' hulls were burned, one of the town's own sons, Aonghas mac Ruairidh, was killed on the strand, and Uilleam Ruadh was taken. Then the harvests failed one on the heels of the last. The reeve's wife Beathag nic Artair died in the hard winter of LE 819, the last households loaded their carts and went inland, and Coinneach, reeve eight-and-forty years, shut his door and took the coast road east. A reeve sent down the empty coast in LE 1,694 counted more berths than households between Baile chrom and Ceann mhòr. Known for the sea-thieves, and the reeve who stayed until the last cart. 315.note: A town of Dia-thìr: the spirit-house of Na Seann Spioradan with the ancestor-posts of the eastern shires; the old Hall. The old hall at Dùn ìseal, where Brìde's flame burns in Talla na Lasrach and the stone cup stands on the threshold, was the heir of the custody before Taigh na Fèithe took it; in this age it is the seat of Na Seann Spioradan of the eastern shires. a young man of Clann Fhearchair, reading them, said a shire that trusted wood to hold its dead must trust its memory further than he would. An earthquake cracked the spirit-house in LE 1,649 and killed no one; the keepers took it for a warning and could not agree of what. Known for the ancestor-posts and Brìde's flame. 316.note: A grove village of Dia-thìr. Its people keep the rite of Òrd Mhacha. The granary village on the road south of the ford had given carts and coal to Taigh na Fèithe without complaint for as long as anyone remembered, and did nothing to deserve what it got in LE 555, save stand on the road Raghnall Ruadh's broken host had to pass. The retreating men took what grain the granary held, fired it and a dozen houses about it, and went on. Coinneach mac Ailein carried his daughter Seònaid and the year's seed-corn out of the fire. Forty-one households walked six days south and wintered at Cathair mhòr on the charity of Macha's temple, where the fire went out in the winter of the refusal; Seònaid grew up to write Leabhar nan Trì Tagraichean. The village was rebuilt, and its people kept the tale of Na Teallaichean Fuara longer than any other in the island. Known for the burning of LE 555, and the child who wrote its history. Both households set every road between the two halves of the island under one following's watch or the other, and carters who had crossed freely all their lives had to say plainly whose peace they travelled under. The old road-house Am Buabhall Fortanach stands by it on the road south, rebuilt in stone by Eilidh nic Chaluim after it burned to its footings in LE 164, where a boy of Clann Fhearchair was given a bowl of the jugged buffalo before the roof was on; Catrìona Bhuadhach's stone road went past it to Inis thais. 326.note: A mill village of Dia-thìr. Its people keep the rite of Òrd an t-Seabhaig. The southern mill town became the southernmost house of Òrd an t-Seabhaig in the sixth century of the count. Its bell-founders cast the first bronze bell on Dia-thìr to hang in a hawk-house in LE 514, with King Tormod Bàn standing at the casting; it cracked in its first frost, and the second, thicker at the waist, held, and rang at every measured burning. There Òrd an t-Seabhaig's teaching was still given whole and unsoftened when it faded elsewhere, and pilgrims came to it from further south than any hawk-house had drawn from before. The southernmost house of Òrd an t-Seabhaig; its bell rings at each measured burning. Known for the first bell of a hawk-house. She wrote it down in a hand her mother taught her, and pupils copied her tracts for households too far to hear her. When Taigh na Fèithe burned some hundred of them in its yard in LE 484 she walked there to see it done and said nothing. One hide in her mother's hand stayed whole in a hollow beam of her house. She died here in LE 505, teaching within the hour of her death, and was buried behind her own house; Coinneach Odhar read the tracts at her grave from the copy he had carried thirty years. Known for Eilidh Dhubh and her tracts. 354.note: A mill village of Dia-thìr. Its people keep the rite of Òrd Mhacha. The town eight miles from Muileann dhearg below the mountain was a custodians' town of Clann Raghnaill, whose households kept galleries there. The hosts of Catrìona nic Aonghais and Dùghall Garbh, joined for the purpose, met Raghnall Ruadh below it in LE 560, and Raghnall fell on the field; the next morning his own custodians struck the seal from Taigh na Fèithe store without waiting to be told who now held the mountain. Dùghall took a cut below the arm there that he hid from his physicians and died of it. Three centuries later the heads of Na Seachd Taighean, sitting five years at Taigh na Fèithe to choose a king, spoke the name of Dòmhnall Ruadh of Muileann chrom, who kept three galleries there, and he spent his first night as king naming which of his neighbours he trusted to measure them honestly in his absence. He came back as king to settle a boundary between two households by asking each one's oldest member where they had played as children. 419.note: A mill village of Dia-thìr. The hill town of the silver seam keeps the sacred wood of Flidais, where the elder teachers of Scoiltean nan Draoidhean met, and its smiths beat the silver neck-rings that the heads of Na Seachd Taighean first wore in LE 149, so that a stranger might know a custodian by the collar before a word was said. Beathag nic Ruairidh taught in its grove when Coinneach mac Mhàrtainn came to it with the question he had carried on the roads, and told him the schools wanted a fixed ground where it might be argued whole. From LE 479 the schools kept the wood and walked its bounds each year in a procession open to anyone who would walk with them. Twice in the age Clann Choinnich asked that the coal be burned beyond the handful to smelt the silver here, in LE 1,559 and in LE 1,776, and twice the council refused; the second time by a single turned vote. Known for the silver collars, the wood of Flidais, and the smelt refused.

420.note: A farm town of Dia-thìr. Its people keep the rite of Òrd Mhanannain. The shire seat a little north of Cuan shean raised the sail-cloth for the fleet. Its tally-keeper cut a notch on his sticks for every close-woven length delivered from the households of Siorrachd Baile àrsaidh, owed once and reckoned against nothing, and by the ninth year he had cut more notches than he had thought the shire held households, some from weavers with no kin on the roll and no thought of sailing. The sticks filled a chest that wanted a second lid. After the sailing the shire went back to weaving for its own backs and the coasting trade, and the levy-chest is remembered in the shire as the one thing it ever gave that it did not count the cost of. Known for the sail-cloth levy for the fleet. Told of in: The sail-cloth tallies at Baile àrsaidh (LE 9).

Queen Sìleas summoned their head to a cold supper at An Talla Dearg; neither spoke of the walls, both understood, and the walls stood. The smiths of the city made the ceremonial blades of the custodian houses from the layered steel of their fellowship, folded and refolded, until in LE 1,568 the fellowship lost the last smith who knew the folding well enough to finish a blade alone; the blades made after him were ordinary work. Known for the walls of Clann Ìomhair, and the layered steel lost. A laden barge out of the new harbour struck the reef in the narrows called Coinneachadh na h-Amhaich in its first year and went down with half her salt, both crewmen swimming ashore; the harbour-masters set the channel's first withy at the rock the next spring. 466.note: A mill village of Dia-thìr. The south-eastern mill town took the swallowing cough in LE 1,079, a sickness that closed the throat until a man could not swallow his own spit; it went house by house along the lower street and up into the hill lanes, and the town lost near a third of its people. Beathag Fhionn, crowned in LE 1,082, shut the coast road between Seann Bhral and Muileann dhomhain within the month and set a reeve at each of its six fords, and the road stayed shut three years; the cough never crossed west of them. 489.note: A town of Dia-thìr: the port of the fleet: Rolla nan Deònach, the first keel, the west quay renamed Cidhe an Diosail; the seat of Òrd Mhanannain. Its people keep the rite of Òrd Mhanannain. The river port at the mouth of the Abhainn naomh was the town a' Scaradh was made in. In its harbour-house, Taigh a' Chalaidh, Calum mac Nèill opened Rolla nan Deònach in the second year and wrote every household whole or not at all, cutting a struck name through with one stroke rather than scraping it. Alasdair Saor laid the first deep keel on the strand below the town, the fellowship of the strand swore its apprentices over a coal, and the queen's masons lengthened the west quay in dressed stone for what the crown called the harbour's trade. On the night before the sailing a lamp stood in every window along the waterfront, and in the morning Calum's grandson Niall cut one notch on a hazel stick for every hull that went round the river pool sunwise and down to the sea. The quay was called Cidhe an Diosail after that, and its old name passed to a fish-wharf. The harbour carried half its old trade within a generation. Mànas mac Ruairidh preached Manannan on its stones in the seventh century of the count, and Taigh Mhanannain was raised beside the harbour-court. Its synod set the prayer for the shut sea at the foot of the river pool. Oidhche nan Lòchran thinned household by household until one old woman, Ealasaid nic Iain, kept the last lamp; eleven people stood on the quay at the last Deas-ghnàth a' Chalaidh Fhalaimh the age records, and the harbour scribe Eòghann mac Nèill counted them. Known for Rolla nan Deònach, Cidhe an Diosail and Oidhche nan Lòchran. 491.note: A town of Dia-thìr. Taigh na Fèithe above the town: keeper of Crom's stone and Leabhar a' Chùraim, heir to Coimheadaichean na Lasrach' Hall; Clachan a' Chrannchuir; Dòmhnall Ruadh's grave. Its people keep the rite of Òrd Bhrìde. Coal-breakers of the central diggings settled below the gate of Taigh na Fèithe, in the first years of the age, and Taigh na Fèithe above them kept Leabhar a' Chùraim, Crom's stone in its inner room, and the lamp in the niche that was never let go out. The custodians counted Rolla nan Deònach against the book here in the third year, nine days at the long table, and found one hearth in five of the coal-right meant to go; here they ruled one sealed measure of coal to each hull that should be ready, and the boy-clerk Donnchadh mac Thormoid made the fair copy at fifteen and began, at thirty, the count of years from An Diosal that the crown took up after him. Na Seachd Taighean were sworn before Crom's stone in LE 55 and drew their galleries by lot in the hall in LE 109. Eachann Briseadair's household built the first stone house below the gate, and the row became a town with its own well, smith and reeve in his lifetime. Eilidh Dhubh's tracts were burned in Taigh na Fèithe yard in LE 484; Raghnall Ruadh refused the handful to the shires that stood against him from its store in LE 558, and Riaghailt an Teallaich was drafted in the same yard seven years later. Dòmhnall Ruadh joined the crown to the mastery of Taigh na Fèithe, and was buried at his own wish in a worked-out gallery with an unlit lamp at his head. Queen Gormshuil rode up to the winter burning here in LE 1,795, as she had every winter of her reign, and nothing more is told. Known for Taigh na Fèithe and Leabhar a' Chùraim. 5.note: Rebuilt in stone by Eilidh nic Chaluim, already known for its jugged buffalo; Rathad na Banrighinn runs past it. Told of in: Am Buabhall Fortanach rebuilt in stone (LE 164); Catrìona's road south (LE 584).

6.note: Feeds the queen's progress with pan-fried spinach and black wine. Told of in: An Taigh-òsta Grianach's spinach (LE 1,786).

7.note: Oatcakes fried in linseed oil and fire water for the coal-carters; its keeper fined for watering the fire water. Told of in: An Leòmhann Buidhe on the north road (LE 304).

8.note: Snowed in a whole season with a party of custodians' reeves inside. Told of in: An Taigh-seinnse Reòta (LE 1,349).

9.note: Syrupped beef for the custodians' reeves on their rounds. Told of in: An Taigh-seinnse Òir's beef (LE 1,339).

10.note: Where the ox-teams wait out the snow; the brothers made their peace under its roof. Told of in: Winter at An Taigh-seinnse Mòr (LE 509); The brothers' peace at An Taigh-seinnse Mòr (LE 1,276).

11.note: Chartered with the seven great road-houses; the keepers settle their accounts here each year. Told of in: The inns of the mining roads chartered (LE 1,319).

12.note: A driftwood fire over the thinned north-western coast. Told of in: The fire at Baile chrom relit (FE 409).

13.note: A driftwood and seal-fat fire. Told of in: The light at Baile ìseal (FE 1,735).

14.note: A driftwood fire kept by fisher-families. Told of in: The light at Muileann bheag (FE 1,735).

15.note: The way in toward Seann Tarr, whose harbour is gone. Told of in: The light at Àth dhearg (FE 1,735); The grey storm at Seann Tarr (LE 1,399).

16.note: The first sea-light raised above the ground; the village below roofed in slate after its fire. Told of in: The light at Tobar dhearg rebuilt (FE 2,883); Fire at Tobar dhearg (LE 446).

17.note: Iain Ciar defeated Alasdair Bàn here and took him alive (LE 1,274). Told of in: The battle of Muileann ghlas (LE 1,274).

19.note: Quarrymen broke into it and found a stair going down beyond their lamps; the custodians walled it up. The one who went down never told. Told of in: The stair at Toll-dubh (LE 979).

20.note: Found again by charcoal-burners, with the same cut stair; walled up, and its entry bound in Leabhar a' Chùraim to the other's. Told of in: The eastern Toll-dubh (LE 1,469).

21.note: Seen near enough to foul the nets of the thinned north-west coast. Told of in: The Sea-Watcher off the north-west (LE 1,199).

22.note: The shepherds light no fires on the high pastures and at last forsake them; a reeve sent to make them see sense does not stay the night. Told of in: The Hollow Man spoken of again (LE 394); The high pastures of Doire uaine forsaken (LE 949).

23.note: Kept by the druids of the schools, who walk its bounds each year: the one open rite of the schools. Told of in: The druid schools keep Coille Naomh Muileann chiar (LE 479).

24.note: Its custody passed by royal grant to the priests of Macha; the other claimants left without contest. Told of in: Macha's priests in Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag (LE 471).

25.note: Boats out of the small islands rob the coasting traders; a force of Queen Eilidh Bhàn burned their boats on Eilean dhubh and hanged Uilleam Ruadh. Told of in: The sea-thieves of the north-west (LE 784); The raid on Eilean dhubh (LE 801).

26.note: The raiders' islets of the east (no raid recorded in this age). Told of in: Raiders in the eastern waters (FE 2,455).

27.note: The north-western strands, thinly held since the dearth. Told of in: The dearth on the north-west shore (LE 819).

28.note: The priests of Òrd an t-Seabhaig cleared its moss and tried to read it, and wrote down that they tried. Told of in: The obelisk at Carragh Cnoc bheag cleaned (LE 1,034).

29.note: Cuimhnich an teine. Told of in: Colbh Cnoc chiar raised (VE 4,770).

30.note: The column of the saying. Told of in: Calbh Cnoc ghorm raised (VE 4,851).

31.note: Measured into Ailean mac Dhùghaill's tables of the old ruins. Told of in: Ailean's tables of the old ruins (LE 1,011).

32.note: Measured into Ailean mac Dhùghaill's tables. Told of in: Ailean's tables of the old ruins (LE 1,011).

33.note: Measured by Ailean mac Dhùghaill: the altar faces the central mountains and not the sea. Told of in: Ailean measures Làrach an Teampaill (LE 999).

34.note: Beathag nic Thòmais's loft over her mill, bought copies of Leabhar a' Chùraim and Rolla a' Chalaidh; the three copies of the landfall tidings side by side. Told of in: Beathag nic Thòmais gathers the old copies (LE 1,659); Three copies of the landfall tidings (LE 1,679); The loft at Muileann chaol (LE 1,699).

37.note: The stone-walled field at Ceann leathan (the games are not recorded in this age). Told of in: The contest at Ceann leathan in stone (FE 2,819).

38.note: The merchants of the long city go to it as one company. Told of in: The market charter of Cathair fhada (LE 287).

39.note: The ferry family's landing; Slighe-mhara Caol fhiadhaich of the Caol fhiadhaich fishers ends here. Told of in: The ferry at Cidhe Beag (LE 1,619); The southern lane (LE 1,389).

40.note: Imrich nam Pantar kept by the southern shires in writing; the panther year of LE 1,729 kept flocks in folds from Cnoc àrsaidh to the coast. Told of in: The crossing days of the panthers (LE 304); The panther year (LE 1,729).

41.note: The custodian houses bury their heads here among graves older than any name on them. Told of in: The houses bury at Tuam Cnoc dhìreach (LE 1,579).

44.note: The headmen of Caol gharbh and Caol chrom settle the dues of the strait at Coinneachadh na h-Amhaich. Told of in: The stone on the neck (LE 1,169).

46.note: Coinneachadh nan Cupan. Told of in: The meeting of the cups (GE 2,408).

48.note: Binnean a' Chlachair. Told of in: The snowflake coal takes fire in the air (VE 2,170).

add.name: Cidhe an Diosail
add.note: The west quay the fleet sailed from, lengthened in dressed stone; renamed so that trade might go on under the old name. Deas-ghnàth a' Chalaidh Fhalaimh and the prayer for the shut sea are kept here on one day. Told of in: The west quay lengthened (LE 30); The Setting-Out (LE 40); The sunwise turn (LE 40); The west quay renamed (LE 67); Cidhe an Diosail (LE 67); Manannan's harbour prayer (LE 1,714).

add.name: Taigh na Fèithe and its lot-stones
add.note: Keeper of Crom's stone and Leabhar a' Chùraim; Clachan a' Chrannchuir for the galleries kept in a bag and shown to visitors; the seal of the trellis and the hollow stone. Told of in: The custodians count the cost (LE 3); The mountain divided among the houses (LE 109); The custody's seal on the king's letters (LE 865).

add.name: the spirit-house and the ancestor-posts
add.note: Burned by lightning and cut again from memory; cracked by the earthquake of LE 1,649. Told of in: The spirit-house at Dùn ìseal (LE 179); The ancestor-posts of Dùn ìseal burned (LE 1,149); Earthquake at Dùn ìseal (LE 1,649).

add.name: the temple of Lia Fàil
add.note: The first temple to Òrd na Cloiche by name, roofed with slate brought by sea. Told of in: Clach first preached at Inis thais (LE 409); The wolf-house at Inis thais (LE 419).

add.name: Macha's great house
add.note: The largest roofed building of the age; its floor of black and white eleven years in the laying. Told of in: Macha's great house at Cathair mhòr (LE 1,459).

add.name: the house of Òrd an t-Seabhaig and Leabhar an t-Seabhaig
add.note: Gormshuil nic Artair's first house; An Seabhag Acrach kept it after the schism. Told of in: Gormshuil of the Hawk (LE 229); The sayings of Gormshuil written (LE 251); The schism of the Hawk (LE 889).

add.name: the ford of Àth shean
add.note: Dùghall Garbh broke Raghnall Ruadh's host; some three hundred dead, most drowned in the ford. Told of in: The ford at Àth shean (LE 554).

add.name: Sèist Cathair dhomhain
add.note: Taken after forty days when the dead of the siege lines fouled its wells; the garrison freed on oath. Told of in: The siege of Cathair dhomhain (LE 557).

add.name: Blàr Muileann chrom
add.note: Raghnall Ruadh fell here; his own custodians opened Taigh na Fèithe the next day. Told of in: The battle of Muileann chrom (LE 560).

add.name: Blàr Cnoc naomh
add.note: The battle that named Cogadh nam Bràithrean. Told of in: The battle of Cnoc naomh (LE 1,270).

add.name: Clach nan Ceithir Ainmean Deug
add.note: At the mouth of the fallen gallery of Cill ghlas. Told of in: The gallery at Cill ghlas (LE 929).

add.name: the salt pans of Ros fhionn
add.note: Brine springs on the river flats; Ros fhionn salt was the measure of worth in the north-east. Told of in: Salt pans at Ros fhionn (LE 354); The salt fair at Ros fhionn (LE 959).

add.name: the paper mill
add.note: The first paper on Dia-thìr, made from rags; Leabhar a' Chùraim first copied onto paper. Told of in: The paper mill at Muileann chaol (LE 1,674).

add.name: the burned sea-thieves' boats
add.note: Queen Eilidh Bhàn's force burned the boats on the strand of Eilean dhubh. Told of in: The raid on Eilean dhubh (LE 801).

add.name: the gates of Seann Warr
add.note: The grant of its own gates and tolls cut over the landward gate. Told of in: Seann Warr's gates honoured (LE 594).

add.name: the felled grove of Doire fhionn
add.note: Felled for the keels of the fleet and drawn to the coast on ox-sleds; it never grew again. Told of in: The oaks of Doire fhionn (LE 5); The coppice law of Doire fhionn (LE 109).

add.name: Taigh na Deasbaid at Dùn thais
add.note: Carson an làmh seo? argued by rule; shut for a generation after Clàr nam Bliadhnachan. Told of in: The house of disputation at Dùn thais (LE 314); The table of years at Dùn thais (LE 1,209); The table forbidden (LE 1,219); The house at Dùn thais reopened (LE 1,759).

add.name: the timber from beyond Ceò Mhanannain
add.note: Longer than any tree on the island, with nails no smith knows; carried to Seann Skell and burned. Told of in: Timber out of the mist (LE 1,794).

3.note: A crown coal-road over the pass by Muileann fhada, posted with the crown's sign; fresh horses at the waypoint houses. Told of in: The coal-roads kept by the crown (LE 939).

16.note: The carriers' road down to Cathair dhearg, a crown coal-road (metalled and named Rathad na Mèinne by the Company in AE 34). Told of in: The coal-roads kept by the crown (LE 939); The crown's riders (LE 944).

17.note: A crown coal-road south from the hills by Muileann chrom. Told of in: The coal-roads kept by the crown (LE 939).

39.note: The carriers' road down to Cathair dhearg, a crown coal-road (metalled and named Rathad na Mèinne by the Company in AE 34). Told of in: The coal-roads kept by the crown (LE 939); The crown's riders (LE 944).

52.note: The carriers' road down to Cathair dhearg, a crown coal-road (metalled and named Rathad na Mèinne by the Company in AE 34). Told of in: The coal-roads kept by the crown (LE 939); The crown's riders (LE 944).

70.note: The carriers' road down to Cathair dhearg, a crown coal-road (metalled and named Rathad na Mèinne by the Company in AE 34). Told of in: The coal-roads kept by the crown (LE 939); The crown's riders (LE 944).

98.note: A crown coal-road down to the southern Seann Skell. Told of in: The coal-roads kept by the crown (LE 939).

111.note: The carriers' road down to Cathair dhearg, a crown coal-road (metalled and named Rathad na Mèinne by the Company in AE 34). Told of in: The coal-roads kept by the crown (LE 939); The crown's riders (LE 944).

115.note: The carriers' road down to Cathair dhearg, a crown coal-road (metalled and named Rathad na Mèinne by the Company in AE 34). Told of in: The coal-roads kept by the crown (LE 939); The crown's riders (LE 944).

130.note: The carriers' road down to Cathair dhearg, a crown coal-road (metalled and named Rathad na Mèinne by the Company in AE 34). Told of in: The coal-roads kept by the crown (LE 939); The crown's riders (LE 944).

131.note: The carriers' road down to Cathair dhearg, a crown coal-road (metalled and named Rathad na Mèinne by the Company in AE 34). Told of in: The coal-roads kept by the crown (LE 939); The crown's riders (LE 944).

173.note: Queen Catrìona's road south from the capital by Baile shean and Am Buabhall Fortanach, laid with stone. Told of in: Catrìona's road south (LE 584).

175.note: Queen Catrìona's road south from the capital by Baile shean and Am Buabhall Fortanach, laid with stone. Told of in: Catrìona's road south (LE 584).

210.note: Queen Catrìona's road south from the capital by Baile shean and Am Buabhall Fortanach, laid with stone. Told of in: Catrìona's road south (LE 584).

229.note: Queen Catrìona's road south from the capital by Baile shean and Am Buabhall Fortanach, laid with stone. Told of in: Catrìona's road south (LE 584).

233.note: Queen Catrìona's road south from the capital by Baile shean and Am Buabhall Fortanach, laid with stone. Told of in: Catrìona's road south (LE 584).

248.note: Queen Catrìona's road south from the capital by Baile shean and Am Buabhall Fortanach, laid with stone. Told of in: Catrìona's road south (LE 584).

354.note: The fishers of Caol fhiadhaich along the whole south coast and up the Abhainn uaine to Cidhe Beag. Told of in: The southern lane (LE 1,389).

403.note: The salt boats of Ros fhionn round the north-east cape; the eastern boats keep it after the pans fail. Told of in: Seòlaid Ros fhionn (LE 1,189).

446.note: The carriers' road down to Cathair dhearg, a crown coal-road (metalled and named Rathad na Mèinne by the Company in AE 34). Told of in: The coal-roads kept by the crown (LE 939); The crown's riders (LE 944).

447.note: Queen Catrìona's road south from the capital by Baile shean and Am Buabhall Fortanach, laid with stone. Told of in: Catrìona's road south (LE 584).

add.name: the cairned drove road of Àth chiar
add.note: The drovers of Àth chiar drive cattle over the eastern hills to the mining towns each year: the first roads on the island marked with cairns. Told of in: The drovers of Àth chiar (LE 484).

add.name: the grain barges down the Abhainn dhomhain
add.note: Forty-one barges counted at the bridge carrying the fleet's grain to the capital, on by the coast to Ros àrsaidh and up the Abhainn naomh to Seann Skell. Told of in: Grain down Abhainn dhomhain (LE 38).

1.note: Harvest after harvest failed; families left for the inland shires and the east. A reeve later counted fewer households than berths. Told of in: The dearth on the north-west shore (LE 819); The north-west coast counted (LE 1,694).

3.note: Three wells cracked; later a gallery fell and killed fourteen. Told of in: The wells crack at Cill ghlas (LE 379); The gallery at Cill ghlas (LE 929).

2.note: Three dry seasons; the crown carted grain in from the south; the wells shared by lot and by turn. Told of in: The dry years at Achadh shean (LE 1,479); The water-rights of Achadh shean (LE 1,489).

4.note: A great swell with no storm took two children; An Gàire Dubh and a second flood at Cuan dhearg. Told of in: Wave at Cnoc chaol (LE 724); An Gàire Dubh (LE 519); Cuan dhearg flooded again (LE 1,754).

add.name: Ceò Mhanannain on the eastern sea
add.note: Hides Dia-thìr from every ship beyond it since the fleet sailed into it; thinner each winter at the close of the age. Told of in: The Setting-Out (LE 40); Manannan preached at Seann Skell (LE 654); The mist thins (LE 1,813).

add.name: Rolla nan Deònach and Am Falbh (LE 2–40)
add.note: The willing entered on boards at Seann Skell by household; nearly one household in five of the coal-right went; nineteen hulls (or twenty-one). Told of in: The Choosing (LE 1); The roll of the willing (LE 2); The custodians count the cost (LE 3); The fleet assembled (LE 38); The Setting-Out (LE 40).

add.name: the cold hearths of Cogadh nan Trì Tagraichean (LE 558)
add.note: Raghnall Ruadh, holding Taigh na Fèithe, denied the handful to every hearth and temple in the shires that stood against him. Told of in: The hearths refused (LE 558).

add.name: the swallowing cough and the closed coast road (LE 1,079–1,082)
add.note: From Muileann dhomhain along the coast road to Seann Bhral; the queen closed the road and set reeves at the fords. Told of in: The swallowing cough at Muileann dhomhain (LE 1,079); The cough at Seann Bhral (LE 1,081); Queen Beathag Fhionn closes the roads (LE 1,082).

add.name: Cogadh nam Bràithrean
add.note: The houses divided four to three between Iain Ciar and Alasdair Bàn. Told of in: Death of King Ailean mac Raghnaill (LE 1,266); The battle of Cnoc naomh (LE 1,270); The fire at Ceann mhin (LE 1,272); The battle of Muileann ghlas (LE 1,274); The brothers' peace at An Taigh-seinnse Mòr (LE 1,276).

add.name: the coppice shires (LE 109)
add.note: No living oak felled without the reeve's mark in every shire with a Doire in its name. Told of in: The coppice law of Doire fhionn (LE 109).

add.name: the salt country of Ros fhionn (LE 354–1,179)
add.note: Ros fhionn salt the common measure of worth in the north-eastern shires. Told of in: Salt pans at Ros fhionn (LE 354); The salt fair at Ros fhionn (LE 959); The silting of Ros fhionn (LE 1,159).

add.name: the lordship of Seann Chwen for life (LE 1,276–1,291)
add.note: Given to Alasdair Bàn at the brothers' peace; returned to the crown at his death. Told of in: The brothers' peace at An Taigh-seinnse Mòr (LE 1,276); Death of Alasdair Bàn (LE 1,291).

add.name: Caol gharbh
add.note: Ground the sea has taken. Told of in: Caol gharbh loses the salt (LE 1,734).
The departed: north-about, beyond the mist. Told of in: The Setting-Out (LE 40); Two landfalls (LE 44).

add.text: A Mhanannain, cùm a' mhuir dùinte
add.note: Manannan, keep the sea shut. Told of in: The synod of Manannan's order (LE 1,590).

add.text: Dh'fhalbh iad, agus cha do dh'fhalbh iad
add.note: They went, and they did not go. Told of in: The rite of the empty harbour (LE 61).
